the social network is a sharp, restless, and surprisingly human drama about ambition, betrayal, and the strange loneliness that can follow success. directed by david fincher, the film adapts ben mezzrich's book and aaron sorkin's screenplay with a pace that feels like a legal thriller, a campus story, and a tech origin myth all at once. its central engine is the relationship between mark zuckerberg and eduardo saavedra, played with electric intensity by jesse eisenberg and andrew garfield. eisenberg's mark is not a hero in the traditional sense; he is brilliant, wounded, impatient, and often cruel, yet the film makes him understandable without making him sympathetic. that balance is one of the movie's greatest strengths.

the script is the film's most distinctive feature. aaron sorkin's dialogue is fast, witty, and often cutting, turning conversations into duels. the famous opening scene, in which mark is rejected by erica albright and then builds facebook as a kind of revenge, is both funny and revealing. the movie understands that the creation of a social network is not just a technical achievement but an emotional one: it is about who gets to define connection, status, and belonging. the legal battles that follow are handled with enough clarity to keep the audience engaged, even when the plot moves quickly between timelines and locations.

visually, fincher keeps the film sleek and controlled. the cold blue tones, the precise framing, and the constant sense of motion give the story a modern, almost clinical feel. this suits the subject matter, because the film is interested in the way technology can make human relationships feel transactional. the soundtrack, including the band's "bittersweet symphony," adds a layer of irony and melancholy, reminding the viewer that the story is not simply a celebration of innovation.

the supporting cast is strong. rosalind craig is excellent as mark's mother, giving the film its most emotionally grounded moments. justin timberlake brings a cool, detached charm to noah glaser, while max minghella is memorable as chris zuckerberg, the brother whose loyalty is tested by the company's rise. the film's ensemble work helps prevent the story from becoming a simple villain-and-victim tale.

in the end, the social network is less interested in who was right or wrong in the lawsuit than in what success costs. its final image of mark alone in a crowded space is one of the most effective endings in recent drama. the movie is intelligent, stylish, and emotionally complex, though some viewers may find its characters too sharp-edged or its legal plot too compressed. still, it remains a powerful portrait of a moment when a small idea became a global force, and of the personal fractures that can happen along the way.

The reality of disability is often reduced to a single image: a person in a wheelchair, a cane, a hearing aid, or a visible difference. But disability is far more complex than any one symbol. It is a lived experience shaped by bodies, minds, environments, policies, culture, and the attitudes of the people around us.

For many people, disability is not a temporary setback but a permanent part of identity. It may be present from birth, or it may arrive later through illness, injury, aging, or accident. Some disabilities are visible, such as mobility impairments or limb differences. Others are invisible, such as chronic pain, mental health conditions, neurological differences, or fatigue that no one can see but that deeply affects daily life.

One of the most important realities of disability is that it is not simply a medical condition. A person’s diagnosis is only one part of the story. The other part is how society responds. A wheelchair user may face a building with no ramp. A person with a visual impairment may struggle with digital tools that are not accessible. A person with a mental health disability may encounter stigma in the workplace or in healthcare. These barriers often matter as much as the disability itself.

Disability also challenges common assumptions about independence. Many people with disabilities live independently, work, raise families, create art, lead organizations, and contribute to their communities. Yet they may still be treated as if they need constant help, protection, or inspiration. The phrase “inspiration porn” exists for a reason: reducing a person’s life to a story of overcoming can feel dismissive. Most people do not want to be admired for surviving; they want to be treated as full human beings with ordinary needs, ambitions, and rights.

Access is central to the reality of disability. Access is not a favor. It is a requirement for participation. This includes physical access, such as ramps, elevators, and accessible restrooms. It also includes communication access, such as captions, sign language interpreters, plain language, and readable digital formats. It includes economic access, because disability often comes with higher costs for transportation, assistive technology, personal care, and medical care. Without access, even capable and determined people can be excluded from education, employment, housing, and public life.

The reality of disability also includes intersectionality. A disabled person’s experience is shaped by race, gender, sexuality, age, class, immigration status, and other identities. A Black woman with a disability may face different barriers than a white man with the same condition. A disabled immigrant may struggle with language access and discrimination. A disabled person living in poverty may have fewer options for care and support. Disability does not exist in a vacuum; it overlaps with other systems of power and inequality.

There is also a reality that disability is not always a personal tragedy. Many people in the disability community reject the idea that their lives are defined by suffering. Disability culture has its own history, humor, art, activism, and pride. The social model of disability reminds us that people are disabled not only by their bodies or minds, but by environments that fail to accommodate human diversity. When a city is built for everyone, when schools provide reasonable accommodations, when employers value different ways of working, and when healthcare providers listen to patients, disability becomes less of a barrier and more of a natural part of human variation.

Still, the reality of disability includes pain, uncertainty, and loss. Many people grieve the life they expected before a diagnosis or injury. Some face medical systems that are slow, dismissive, or focused on “fixing” them rather than supporting them. Some are isolated by distance, cost, or lack of transportation. Some are cared for by people who love them but do not fully understand their needs. The emotional reality can be as demanding as the physical one.

At the same time, disability can bring clarity. It can teach patience, creativity, and a sharp awareness of what matters. It can strengthen relationships and build communities of mutual support. It can also reveal how fragile able-bodied assumptions really are. Most people, if given the right support, can live meaningful lives. The question is not whether disability limits a person, but whether society provides the conditions for that person to thrive.

The reality of disability, then, is not a single story. It is a mosaic of bodies, barriers, rights, relationships, and resilience. It asks us to move beyond pity, inspiration, or fear, and toward something more practical: respect, access, and inclusion. Disability is not a problem to be solved. It is a part of human life that calls for a more thoughtful and just world.

# The Best Way to Get a Good Night’s Sleep

If you’ve ever lain awake at 2 a.m., staring at the ceiling and wondering why sleep won’t come, you’re not alone. Sleep is one of the most important parts of daily life, yet it’s also one of the easiest things to neglect. The good news is that you don’t need a fancy mattress, a perfect bedroom, or a complicated routine to sleep better. The best way to get a good night’s sleep is to build a simple, consistent habit that supports your body’s natural rhythm.

Start with consistency. Your body loves routine. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day, even on weekends, helps regulate your internal clock. When your body knows what to expect, it becomes easier to fall asleep and wake up feeling refreshed. If you find yourself struggling to fall asleep, try going to bed a little earlier for a few nights until your body adjusts.

Next, create a calming pre-sleep routine. The last hour before bed is a great time to slow down. Dim the lights, put away your phone, and avoid stimulating activities like intense work, arguments, or fast-paced videos. Instead, try reading a book, taking a warm shower, stretching gently, or listening to soft music. The goal is to send your brain a clear signal: it’s time to wind down.

Your environment matters, too. A good sleep space should be cool, dark, and quiet. Many people sleep best in a room that feels slightly cool, around 60 to 67 degrees Fahrenheit. If light is a problem, use blackout curtains or an eye mask. If noise keeps you awake, try earplugs or a white noise machine. Your bed should also be reserved for sleep and intimacy, not for working, scrolling, or watching TV. This helps your brain associate the bed with rest.

What you consume during the day can also affect your sleep. Caffeine is a common sleep thief, especially if you drink coffee or energy drinks late in the afternoon. Alcohol may make you feel drowsy at first, but it often disrupts sleep later in the night. Heavy meals close to bedtime can also make it harder to rest, so try to finish eating a few hours before you go to sleep.

Don’t underestimate the power of movement. Regular exercise can help you fall asleep faster and sleep more deeply. However, intense workouts too close to bedtime may leave you too energized to relax. If you exercise in the evening, keep it light, such as a walk or gentle yoga.

Finally, manage your thoughts. If your mind races at night, try writing down your worries or tomorrow’s to-do list before bed. This simple habit can help your brain “park” those thoughts so they don’t keep you awake. If you can’t sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm in low light, then return to bed when you feel sleepy.

Getting a good night’s sleep isn’t about perfection. It’s about making small, steady choices that support your body’s need for rest. When you prioritize consistency, calm, and a comfortable environment, sleep becomes less of a struggle and more of a natural part of your day. And when you sleep well, everything else—your mood, energy, focus, and health—tends to improve, too.

**Course Proposal: The History of the World, as Told by Dogs**

**Course Title:** The History of the World, as Told by Dogs  
**Department:** History / Environmental Humanities / Animal Studies  
**Course Level:** Undergraduate, 3000-level  
**Credits:** 3  

**Course Description:**  
This interdisciplinary course examines human history through the experiences, roles, and symbolic lives of dogs. From ancient burial sites to wartime service, from urban policing to companion animals in modern households, dogs have witnessed and shaped social change. The course asks what a canine perspective reveals about power, labor, kinship, and ecology. It also considers how dogs have been used in predatory contexts, including hunting, warfare, and policing, while exploring ethical questions about animal agency and representation.

**Learning Objectives:**  
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. Analyze primary and secondary sources that depict dogs in historical, cultural, and political contexts.  
2. Evaluate how dogs have reflected and influenced human institutions such as the military, the state, the household, and the marketplace.  
3. Critically assess narratives that portray dogs as loyal, dangerous, or predatory.  
4. Develop a historically informed argument about the relationship between animals and human societies.

**Sample Syllabus:**

**Week 1: Dogs and the Origins of Civilization**  
- Early domestication  
- Dogs in ancient burial practices  
- What canine remains tell us about human-animal relationships  

**Week 2: Dogs in the Ancient World**  
- Dogs in Egypt, Greece, and Rome  
- Myth, religion, and the afterlife  
- Dogs as companions, workers, and symbols  

**Week 3: Medieval and Early Modern Dogs**  
- Dogs in monasteries, courts, and households  
- Hunting culture and social status  
- Legal regulations and animal ownership  

**Week 4: Dogs and Empire**  
- Dogs in colonial expansion  
- Military use and imperial control  
- Representation in travel writing and visual culture  

**Week 5: Dogs in War**  
- Messenger dogs, detection dogs, and war memorials  
- The emotional labor of military animals  
- Memory, mourning, and public commemoration  

**Week 6: Dogs, Labor, and the City**  
- Working dogs in industry, transport, and commerce  
- Police dogs and public order  
- Urban space and animal mobility  

**Week 7: Dogs and Science**  
- Experimental animals and medical research  
- Breeding, genetics, and the construction of “pure” dogs  
- Ethical debates in animal experimentation  

**Week 8: Dogs in the Modern Home**  
- Pet ownership and consumer culture  
- Emotional companionship and family life  
- The rise of the “pet humanization” movement  

**Week 9: Dogs, Race, and Social Hierarchy**  
- Breed standards and racial ideology  
- Dogs in propaganda and political imagery  
- Whose dogs are valued, and why?  

**Week 10: Dogs in the Digital Age**  
- Social media, viral dogs, and public affection  
- Technology, tracking, and surveillance  
- New forms of animal visibility  

**Assessment:**  
- Participation and discussion: 15%  
- Short analytical essays: 30%  
- Final research paper: 55%  

For the final research paper, students will investigate a historical episode involving dogs, such as a predatory hunting practice, a wartime service story, or a legal dispute over animal ownership, and argue how it illuminates broader historical processes.

First, start with simple commands like “sit,” “stay,” and “come.” Use a happy voice and give your dog a treat when they do the right thing. Dogs love treats, so this makes training feel like a game.

Next, keep training sessions short. Kids can get excited, and dogs can get tired, so five to ten minutes is a great amount of time. This helps your dog stay focused and makes training less boring for both of you.

Always be gentle. If your dog makes a mistake, don’t get angry. Just say “no” in a calm voice and try again. Dogs learn best when they feel safe and loved.

Practice every day, even if it’s just for a few minutes. Repetition helps your dog remember what you want them to do. You can even make it a family activity, so everyone can help.

When your dog learns a new trick, celebrate! You can clap, cheer, or give them a favorite treat. The finale of your training session should always be fun, so your dog looks forward to the next one.

Remember, training a dog is not about being perfect. It’s about having fun, building trust, and making a special bond. With time and love, your dog will become a happy, well-trained friend.

I was eating by the water,
Sun was low, the sky was blue,
A piece of chicken caught my throat,
And the Potomac looked right through.

I coughed, I gasped, I waved my hand,
The river kept on rolling slow,
A drumstick’s dream, a dinner’s end,
With nowhere left for me to go.

Oh, the willows whispered, “Don’t you choke,
The current’s cold, the current’s deep,”
But I was thinking of the fryer,
And the bread I’d left upon my plate.

The herons stood like silent judges,
The ducks went quack, the fish went by,
I tried to sing a final chorus,
But all I got was “ah-ah-ah.”

So if you see a pale hand floating,
With a bone still caught inside,
Remember me by riverbank,
Where the chicken met the tide.
